title: Generics workshop: a type-safe container and event bus
goal: By the end you can build four small designs that use the whole track: an `Either<out L, out R>` that leans on `Nothing`, a repository with a covariant read view, a typed event bus that stores handlers as adapters, and a container of typed keys that carry a `KType`, and you can say why each type parameter is `out`, `in` or invariant.

warmup.q: `sealed interface Either<out L, out R>` with `data class Left<out L>(val value: L) : Either<L, Nothing>`. In `fun <L, R, R2> Either<L, R>.map(f: (R) -> R2): Either<L, R2>`, can the `Left` branch simply return `this`?
options: No: `this` is an `Either<L, R>`, and the function must return an `Either<L, R2>`
Yes: a `Left<L>` is an `Either<L, Nothing>`, which is an `Either<L, R2>` because `Nothing` is a subtype of `R2` and `R` is `out`
Only with an unchecked cast to `Either<L, R2>`
Only if `R2` is the same type as `R`
warmup.why: After the smart cast, `this` is a `Left<L>`, whose declared supertype is `Either<L, Nothing>`. With `out R`, `Nothing` below `R2` means `Either<L, Nothing>` is below `Either<L, R2>`. So one `Left` object is a valid result for any success type. Java, with no `Nothing`, has to build a new `Left` in that branch.

alt.title: TypedKeysDemoJava.java

try.expect: Both print `currencies = [EUR, USD], retries = 3`. Kotlin then prints `ClassCastException: class java.lang.Integer cannot be cast to class java.util.List`: `leaky[leakyCurrencies] = 42` compiled because `out T` let `T` be inferred as `Any`, and the read failed later. The wrong move fails with `Argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Int', but 'List<String>' was expected.` in Kotlin and `method set in class Attributes cannot be applied to given types` in Java.

analogy: The event bus is a post office sorting room. Letters (events) come in from every counter, which is the producing side. Each pigeonhole is labeled with a letter class, such as "registered", and each pigeonhole has clerks assigned to it, which is the consuming side. A clerk trained to handle any letter can be assigned to the registered pigeonhole: that's the `(PaymentEvent) -> Unit` handler under `CardAuthorized::class`. A clerk who only handles registered letters can't be given the general pile, so the office puts a checker in front of him who passes on only registered mail: that's the `safeCast` adapter. The analogy breaks at the checker. A real clerk would notice a wrong letter himself, but a Kotlin lambda can't: if you skip the adapter and cast the handler instead, the wrong event reaches it and fails with a `ClassCastException` inside the handler.
in_your_world: These four shapes map straight onto a payment service. A Kafka consumer decodes each record and publishes it on an in-process bus, where the fraud check, the ledger writer and the audit log subscribe by event class, and the audit log takes every `PaymentEvent`. Validation of an incoming authorization returns `Either<RejectReason, AuthorizedPayment>` instead of throwing, so a Temporal workflow can branch on it without catching exceptions across the activity boundary. A reporting job that reads merchants and settlements from Oracle takes `ReadRepository<Entity<*>>`, while only the write path sees the invariant `Repository`. And per-request context in a Quarkus endpoint (the merchant id, the accepted currencies, the idempotency key) fits a typed-key container, so `context[IDEMPOTENCY_KEY]` comes back as a `String` with no cast.
mistake: The common mistake in an event bus is casting the handler instead of wrapping it: `handlers.add(handler as (PaymentEvent) -> Unit)` under `@Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST")`. It compiles, and every test that publishes the right event type passes. The first time an event of another class reaches that list, through a shared key, a supertype subscription or a bug in the routing, the handler receives it and throws `ClassCastException: class RefundIssued cannot be cast to class CardAuthorized` from inside its own body, far from the subscription that caused it. People write the cast because the adapter looks like extra ceremony, and because erasure makes the cast itself succeed. The fix is the adapter, `{ event -> type.safeCast(event)?.let(handler) }`, which costs one line and makes the wrong event a no-op.

compare.title: The typed event bus in Java and Kotlin

java.title: EventBus.java

kotlin.title: EventBus.kt

compare.note: The design is the same in both languages: keys from the event's run-time class, handlers stored behind an adapter that checks the class and casts, and a handler parameter that accepts supertypes. Where Java writes the variance at each use (`Class<? extends PaymentEvent>` keys, `Consumer<? super E>` handlers), Kotlin gets it from declarations: `event::class` is already a `KClass<out PaymentEvent>`, and a function type is already `in` on its parameter, so `(E) -> Unit` needs no projection. Kotlin also adds the reified wrapper, which needs `noinline` because the lambda is stored. Java callers can use the `KClass` version only through `JvmClassMappingKt.getKotlinClass(CardAuthorized.class)`, so a bus meant for Java code should also offer a `Class<E>` overload.

worked.title: Route a card-issuer webhook through all four designs

steps.say: A webhook body arrives. 1. Parse it into an `Either` instead of throwing, so the caller decides what a bad body means.

2. Publish the successes on the bus. 3. Record the failures in the request's typed attributes. Self-check before reading the comment: why can `Either.Right(CardAuthorized(...))` be returned where `Either<String, PaymentEvent>` is expected? (`Right<CardAuthorized>` is an `Either<Nothing, CardAuthorized>`, and both parameters are `out`.)

4. Wire the handlers once, at startup. The audit log is a `(PaymentEvent) -> Unit` and subscribes under both event classes; the fraud check only understands card authorizations. A nightly report reads merchants through the covariant `ReadRepository<Entity<*>>` view. Every type parameter in this flow has the variance its role demands, and the only casts are the two that are safe by construction: `safeCast` in the bus adapter and the unchecked cast inside `Attributes.get`.

alt.title: Either.java

recap: `Either<out L, out R>` with `Left : Either<L, Nothing>` lets one `Left` stand for every success type, so `map` can return `this`. Java must rebuild it.
When a type both reads and writes `T`, split out the reading half as an `out T` interface. Readers get covariance; the full type stays invariant and safe.
In an event bus, events are produced and handlers consume. Keys are `KClass<out PaymentEvent>` from `event::class`, and handlers are stored behind a `safeCast` adapter.
A reified wrapper that stores its lambda needs `noinline`.
A typed key carries its value type (`Key<T>` with a `KType` inside), so reads need no cast and same-named keys of different types don't collide.
A key is used to write, so it must be invariant. With `out T`, a wrong value goes in and fails later as a `ClassCastException`.

quiz.q: Which interface can safely be declared with `out T`?
options: `interface Repository<T> { fun save(entity: T): T }`
`interface Cache<T> { var current: T }`
`interface ReadRepository<T> { fun findAll(): List<T> }`
`interface Key<T> { val name: String }`, used as `set(key: Key<T>, value: T)`
quiz.why: `ReadRepository` only hands `T` out. `save` takes a `T`, and a `var` is both read and written, so those must be invariant. The key is the subtle one: it has no `T` member at all, so `out T` would compile, but it is used to choose what may be written, and `out` would let `set(key, 42)` through.

quiz.q: In the event bus, why can't `subscribe` simply do `handlers[type]!!.add(handler)` with `handler: (E) -> Unit` and a list of `(PaymentEvent) -> Unit`?
options: Because lambdas can't be stored in a map
Because `(E) -> Unit` is not a `(PaymentEvent) -> Unit`: function parameters are `in`, and a card-only handler can't take a refund
Because `E` is erased, so the list can't hold it
It can; the adapter is only for performance
quiz.why: A `(PaymentEvent) -> Unit` must accept every event. A handler that only takes `CardAuthorized` doesn't, so the compiler refuses the add. The adapter takes any event and passes on only those that `safeCast` to `E`. The reverse direction works: a `(PaymentEvent) -> Unit` handler is a `(CardAuthorized) -> Unit`.

quiz.q: Why does the reified `subscribe` need `noinline` on its handler parameter?
options: Because reified functions can't take lambdas
Because Java callers need it
Because the handler is stored in the map, so it must exist as an object instead of being inlined
Because `noinline` makes the type parameter reified
quiz.why: Lambdas passed to an inline function are inlined too, so they don't exist as values. A lambda you store, return or pass on to a non-inline function must stay an object, which `noinline` requests. It has nothing to do with `reified`, which is about the type parameter.

quiz.q: `data class Key<T>(val name: String, val type: KType)`. Why include the `KType` when the key already has a name?
options: So that `key<List<Long>>("retries")` and `key<Int>("retries")` are different keys and can't collide
Because a data class needs at least two properties
So that `get` can cast without an unchecked warning
Because `KType` makes the key covariant
quiz.why: With the name alone, two keys with the same name and different value types would share one slot, and reading one would return the other's value. The `KType` from `typeOf<T>()` makes them unequal. The cast in `get` is still unchecked; it is safe because only `set` puts values in.

quiz.q: From "Star projection: when you don't know the type": a metrics helper reports the size of any in-memory buffer, a `MutableList<CardAuthorized>`, a `MutableList<String>` or anything else. Which parameter type fits best?
options: `MutableList<Any?>`
`MutableList<in Any>`
`MutableList<PaymentEvent>`
`MutableList<*>`
quiz.why: The helper neither reads typed elements nor writes any, so a star projection says exactly that and accepts every mutable list. `MutableList<Any?>` accepts only lists whose element type is exactly `Any?`, and `in Any` accepts only lists of `Any` or `Any?`. (A plain `Collection<*>` would be even more general.)

flashcards.front: Why is `Left` declared `Left<out L>(val value: L) : Either<L, Nothing>`?
flashcards.back: So one `Left` fits `Either<L, R>` for every `R`: `Nothing` is a subtype of every type, and `Either` is `out` in `R`.

flashcards.front: A repository both saves and returns `T`. How do you let read-only code accept a repository of any entity?
flashcards.back: Split out `interface ReadRepository<out T> { fun findAll(): List<T> }` and have the full `Repository` extend it. Readers take `ReadRepository<Entity<*>>`.

flashcards.front: What type do the keys of a class-keyed event bus have, and why?
flashcards.back: `KClass<out PaymentEvent>`, because `event::class` on a `PaymentEvent` has exactly that type.

flashcards.front: How do you store a `(CardAuthorized) -> Unit` in a list of `(PaymentEvent) -> Unit`?
flashcards.back: Wrap it: `{ event -> CardAuthorized::class.safeCast(event)?.let(handler) }`. The adapter takes any event and passes on only a `CardAuthorized`.

flashcards.front: When does a lambda parameter of an inline function need `noinline`?
flashcards.back: When the function stores it, returns it or passes it to non-inline code, as `subscribe` does with its handler map.

flashcards.front: Why must a typed `Key<T>` be invariant?
flashcards.back: It decides what may be written. With `out T`, a `Key<List<String>>` could act as a `Key<Any>`, `set(key, 42)` would compile, and the next read would throw `ClassCastException`.

terms.plain: A result that is a failure (`Left`) or a success (`Right`), declared `out` in both.
Splitting a type's reading half into its own covariant interface, so readers get flexibility the full type can't have.
A small wrapper that turns one function type into another, here by checking the event's class first.
Marks a lambda parameter of an inline function that must stay an object, because it is stored.
A key object that carries the type of its value, so a container can return that type without casts.
An unchecked cast that can't fail, because a private invariant guarantees what was stored.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate reviews the lab's `EventBus` and asks two things: why the bus wraps every handler in a lambda instead of storing it directly, and why the audit handler, typed `(PaymentEvent) -> Unit`, can subscribe under `CardAuthorized::class`. Explain both with the producer and consumer picture.
explain_back.answer: Events are produced by publishers and consumed by handlers, so a handler's type is `in` on its parameter. That gives both answers. A handler typed `(CardAuthorized) -> Unit` can only consume card authorizations, so it is not a `(PaymentEvent) -> Unit`, which must consume any event. The bus keeps one list of `(PaymentEvent) -> Unit` per class, so it can't store the card handler as it is. It stores an adapter instead: a function that takes any `PaymentEvent`, checks it with `CardAuthorized::class.safeCast`, and passes it on only if it really is a card authorization. Casting the handler would compile but fail with a `ClassCastException` inside the handler the first time a wrong event arrived. The audit handler goes the other way. It consumes every `PaymentEvent`, so it can certainly consume card authorizations: because the parameter is `in`, a `(PaymentEvent) -> Unit` is a `(CardAuthorized) -> Unit`, and `subscribe(CardAuthorized::class, auditAll)` type-checks with `E = CardAuthorized`.

deeper.body:
Each design has a natural next step.

The bus delivers only to the event's exact class. To deliver a `CardAuthorized` to handlers subscribed under `PaymentEvent::class` too, `publish` must walk the event's supertypes. Without kotlin-reflect you can do that through Java reflection: `event.javaClass.interfaces` and `event.javaClass.superclass`, converted with `.kotlin`. With kotlin-reflect, `KClass.allSuperclasses` lists them directly. Cache the result per class, since the walk is the same every time.

`Either` gets more useful with `flatMap`, which chains steps that can each fail: `fun <L, R, R2> Either<L, R>.flatMap(f: (R) -> Either<L, R2>): Either<L, R2>`. Its `Left` branch returns `this` for the same reason `map` can. The standard library's own `Result<out T>` is also declared `out`, but its failure side is always a `Throwable`; `Either` lets the failure be a domain type such as `RejectReason`. Libraries such as Arrow ship a full `Either`.

The repository can grow a write-only view too: `interface WriteRepository<in T> { fun save(entity: T) }`. A loader that writes `Merchant`s can then accept a `WriteRepository<Entity<Long>>`. With both views, the invariant `Repository` is simply the type that is both.

The typed keys can carry a default: `class Key<T>(val name: String, val type: KType, val default: T)`, with `get` returning `T` instead of `T?`. Keep `Key` invariant when you do: `default` is read, but `set` still writes through the key.
